{"title": "Reading the income statement", "body": {"version": 1, "reading_minutes": 8, "blocks": [{"type": "why_here", "md": "The income statement is the first page of any set of accounts an interviewer will put in front of you, and it is the one statement almost every candidate *thinks* they already understand. That is exactly why it gets asked about. The interviewer is listening for two things: whether you know that **revenue** and **cash received** are different animals, and whether you can walk from the top line to the bottom line without skipping the lines that matter for valuation.

Get this right and the balance sheet and cash flow statement lessons that follow make far more sense, because most of what moves on those two statements starts life here."}, {"type": "concept", "heading": "A film of the year, not a photo", "md": "The income statement records what a company *earned* and what it *used up* over a period, usually a year or a quarter. Think of it as a film of the business running, whereas the balance sheet is a single photograph taken at midnight on the last day.

The key idea underneath it is **accrual accounting**: a sale counts when the goods or service are delivered, not when the customer pays, and a cost counts when the resource is consumed, not when the bill is settled. A window cleaner who finishes a job in March and is paid in May has March **revenue** and a March **receivable**; the cash turns up two months later on a different statement.

Because of accrual accounting, the number at the bottom, **net income**, is a measure of *performance*, not of *cash*. That distinction is the single most examined idea in this whole topic."}, {"type": "mechanics", "md": "Read it top to bottom, and give each subtotal a job.

1. **Revenue** — the value of goods and services delivered in the period.
2. **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** — the direct cost of what was delivered: materials, factory labour, freight in.
3. **Gross profit** = Revenue − COGS. This tells you what the *product* earns before the company spends anything on selling it or running the office.
4. **Operating expenses** — selling, general and administrative costs, research, and **depreciation and amortisation (D&A)** if the company shows it separately.
5. **Operating profit (EBIT)** = Gross profit − Operating expenses. What the *business* earns before anyone who lends to it or taxes it takes a slice.
6. **Net interest** — the cost of the company's debt, less any interest it earns.
7. **Profit before tax** = EBIT − Net interest.
8. **Tax** — usually a rate applied to profit before tax.
9. **Net income** = Profit before tax − Tax. What is left for shareholders.

One formula ties the middle together, and it matters for valuation:

$$\text{EBITDA} = \text{EBIT} + \text{D\&A}$$

where EBIT is operating profit and D&A is the depreciation and amortisation charged in the period. EBITDA is not a line on the statement itself; you build it, because it approximates the operating cash the business throws off before investment and financing choices."}, {"type": "worked_calc", "md": "Kestrel Foods plc, a snack maker, reports the following for the year (all £m): revenue 800, COGS 480, operating expenses 200 (of which D&A is 40), net interest 20, tax rate 25 %. Build the statement.", "steps": [{"label": "Gross profit", "expr": "800 - 480", "value": 320, "unit": "£m"}, {"label": "EBIT", "expr": "320 - 200", "value": 120, "unit": "£m"}, {"label": "EBITDA", "expr": "120 + 40", "value": 160, "unit": "£m"}, {"label": "Profit before tax", "expr": "120 - 20", "value": 100, "unit": "£m"}, {"label": "Tax", "expr": "100 * 25%", "value": 25, "unit": "£m"}, {"label": "Net income", "expr": "100 - 25", "value": 75, "unit": "£m"}]}, {"type": "trap", "md": "**"Net income is the cash the company made this year."** It is not. Net income is struck after non-cash charges such as depreciation, and before the cash effects of building inventory, waiting for customers to pay, or buying equipment. Kestrel could report £75m of net income and see its bank balance fall, if it spent heavily on a new factory or its supermarket customers paid late. The cash story lives on the cash flow statement; the income statement tells you whether the business is *profitable*."}, {"type": "canonical_answer", "md": "The income statement shows a company's revenue and expenses over a period on an accrual basis, so it measures performance rather than cash. Revenue less cost of goods sold gives gross profit; less operating expenses gives operating profit, or EBIT; less interest and tax gives net income for shareholders. Adding depreciation and amortisation back to EBIT gives EBITDA, which is why bankers use the statement so heavily for valuation multiples.", "seconds": 40}, {"type": "your_turn", "prompt": "Harbourline plc reports revenue of £1,200m, COGS of £700m, operating expenses of £300m including D&A of £60m, net interest of £40m and a 20 % tax rate. Give gross profit, EBIT, EBITDA and net income.", "model_answer_md": "Gross profit = 1,200 − 700 = **£500m**.

EBIT = 500 − 300 = **£200m**.

EBITDA = 200 + 60 = **£260m**.

Profit before tax = 200 − 40 = £160m; tax = 160 × 20 % = £32m; net income = **£128m**.", "rubric": ["Gross profit £500m", "EBIT £200m", "EBITDA £260m by adding D&A back to EBIT", "Net income £128m after interest and 20 % tax"]}, {"type": "quick_fire", "pairs": [{"q": "Is the income statement a stock or a flow?", "a": "A flow: it covers a period, unlike the balance sheet snapshot."}, {"q": "When does revenue get recognised?", "a": "When the good or service is delivered, not when the cash arrives."}, {"q": "Which subtotal is before interest and tax?", "a": "Operating profit, also called EBIT."}, {"q": "How do you get EBITDA from the statement?", "a": "Take EBIT and add back depreciation and amortisation."}]}, {"type": "one_liner", "md": "The income statement measures what the business *earned* over a period; whether it *collected* the money is a different statement's job."}, {"type": "now_you_can", "items": ["I can walk from revenue to net income and name every subtotal", "I can explain why net income is not cash", "I can build EBITDA from EBIT and D&A with a number attached"]}, {"type": "widget", "widget": "filings_toggle"}]}}

{"questions": [{"kind": "concept", "difficulty": 1, "question": "What does the income statement show, and over what period?", "model_answer_md": "It shows a company's revenue and expenses over a period, typically a quarter or a year, and the profit left after them. It is prepared on an accrual basis, so revenue is counted when goods or services are delivered and costs when they are consumed, regardless of when cash moves. The bottom line, net income, is what remains for shareholders after cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest and tax.", "key_points": ["Revenue and expenses over a period", "Accrual basis, not cash", "Ends at net income for shareholders"], "follow_ups": [{"question": "How is that different from the balance sheet?", "answer_md": "The balance sheet is a snapshot of what the company owns and owes on one date; the income statement is the activity between two such snapshots."}, {"question": "Name three subtotals on the way down.", "answer_md": "Gross profit, operating profit (EBIT) and profit before tax."}], "weak_answer_note": "Describes it as 'money in and money out' without mentioning accrual timing.", "numbers": null, "tags": ["income statement", "accruals", "definition"], "flashcard_back": null}, {"kind": "concept", "difficulty": 2, "question": "Why do bankers care more about EBITDA than net income when they compare companies?", "model_answer_md": "Because EBITDA strips out the choices that differ between otherwise similar businesses. Net income is after interest, which depends on how much debt each company chose to carry, after tax, which depends on where it operates, and after depreciation, which depends on when it last bought its assets and how it depreciates them. EBITDA sits above all three, so it is closer to the operating cash the business generates and lets you compare a heavily indebted company with a debt-free one on the same footing. That is also why EBITDA pairs with enterprise value rather than equity value.", "key_points": ["Excludes interest, so capital structure does not distort it", "Excludes tax and depreciation policy differences", "Closer to operating cash generation", "Pairs with enterprise value"], "follow_ups": [{"question": "What is EBITDA's main weakness?", "answer_md": "It ignores the capital spending needed to keep the business running, so an asset-heavy company can look cheap on EBITDA while consuming cash on replacement equipment."}, {"question": "Is EBITDA a line on the income statement?", "answer_md": "Usually not. You build it by adding depreciation and amortisation back to operating profit."}], "weak_answer_note": "Says 'it is closer to cash' without naming which items are excluded and why they distort comparisons.", "numbers": null, "tags": ["ebitda", "comparability", "valuation"], "flashcard_back": null}, {"kind": "concept", "difficulty": 3, "question": "A company switches its depreciation policy so that its equipment is written off over 10 years instead of 5. What happens to EBIT, EBITDA and net income in the first year after the change?", "model_answer_md": "The annual depreciation charge halves, so operating expenses fall and **EBIT rises** by the amount saved. **EBITDA is unchanged**, because depreciation is added back to EBIT anyway; the change simply moves a number between two lines that EBITDA ignores. **Net income rises**, but by less than EBIT, because the higher profit before tax attracts more tax: with a 25 % tax rate, a \u00a310m lower depreciation charge lifts net income by \u00a37.5m. Cash is untouched in the year, since depreciation is not a cash cost; the only cash effect is the extra tax paid on the higher profit.", "key_points": ["Depreciation halves, EBIT rises by the saving", "EBITDA unchanged", "Net income rises by the saving less tax", "No cash effect apart from the higher tax bill"], "follow_ups": [{"question": "Does the change make the company more valuable?", "answer_md": "Not in substance: the assets wear out at the same rate and the cash flows are unchanged, so an EV/EBITDA valuation is identical. Only a naive P/E valuation would move."}, {"question": "Where would you see this change disclosed?", "answer_md": "In the accounting policies note, and usually flagged as a change in estimate with its effect on the year's profit."}], "weak_answer_note": "Says all three measures rise, or forgets the tax leakage on the net income effect.", "numbers": null, "tags": ["depreciation", "ebit", "ebitda", "policy change"], "flashcard_back": null}, {"kind": "concept", "difficulty": 4, "question": "Two companies report the same revenue and the same net income, yet one has an EBITDA margin of 30 % and the other 12 %. What could explain the gap, and which would you rather own?", "model_answer_md": "Same net income at very different EBITDA means the high-EBITDA company loses far more between EBITDA and the bottom line. The candidates are heavy depreciation and amortisation, which points to an asset-heavy business or to acquired intangibles being amortised; large interest costs from a lot of debt; or a higher tax rate. The low-EBITDA company is lean above the line but has little debt and light assets.\n\nWhich to own depends on why. If the gap is amortisation of acquired intangibles, it is a non-cash accounting artefact and the 30 % business is generating far more cash. If it is depreciation on plant that must be replaced, the cash advantage is smaller than it looks. If it is interest, the 30 % company is riskier: the same profit sits on a bigger pile of debt. So the honest answer is that you would want the cash flow statement before choosing.", "key_points": ["Gap sits in D&A, interest or tax", "Acquired-intangible amortisation is a non-cash artefact", "Heavy depreciation implies real replacement capex", "High interest means higher leverage and risk", "Cash flow statement decides it"], "follow_ups": [{"question": "Which valuation multiple would make the two look most different?", "answer_md": "EV/EBITDA, where the 30 % company looks far cheaper on the same enterprise value; P/E would show them as identical."}, {"question": "How could you check whether the depreciation reflects real capex needs?", "answer_md": "Compare depreciation with capital expenditure over several years; if capex runs well above depreciation, the assets are being replaced at a higher cost than the charge suggests."}], "weak_answer_note": "Picks the 30 % company outright without asking what sits between EBITDA and net income.", "numbers": null, "tags": ["ebitda margin", "leverage", "d&a", "edge case"], "flashcard_back": "Same net income with different EBITDA means the gap is in D&A, interest or tax \u2014 check which before preferring the high-margin one."}]}
